sg-vs-nacl.title: Security Group vs Network ACL
sg-vs-nacl.summary: Both are VPC firewalls with inbound and outbound rules, but they work at different levels and handle return traffic differently.
pick: Choose a Security Group for normal least-privilege access between instances and tiers.
Choose a Network ACL to explicitly block an IP or CIDR range at the subnet level.

values: Stateless: return traffic needs its own rule
Numbered rules, lowest first, first match wins
New SG: deny all inbound, allow all outbound
Default NACL allows all; custom NACL denies all
CIDR, prefix list, other security groups
Chain tiers by referencing SG IDs

sg-vs-nacl.diagram:
~~~flow
# A request passes the NACL then the SG; the reply skips SG rules but needs a NACL rule
Client -> NACL inbound (subnet) -> Security Group inbound (ENI) -> EC2
EC2 -[response]-> Security Group (stateful, auto-allowed) -> NACL outbound (open 1024-65535) -> Client
~~~

~~~ladder
# A NACL checks rules by number; the first match wins
Rule 100 | Deny 203.0.113.5/32 | Matched first
Rule 200 | Allow 0.0.0.0/0 port 443 | Allow
Rule * | Deny all traffic that matched no rule | Default
~~~

keywords.trigger: Block a specific malicious IP address
keywords.answer: Network ACL Deny rule (or AWS WAF for HTTP)

keywords.trigger: Stateful, allow only
Allow traffic only from the web tier instances
keywords.answer: Security Group referencing the web tier SG

keywords.trigger: Outbound response traffic blocked at subnet

iam-policy-types.title: IAM policy types
iam-policy-types.summary: All are JSON policies, but only some grant permissions; boundaries and SCPs only set the maximum allowed.
pick: Choose an identity-based policy to give a user, group or role permissions.
Choose a resource-based policy to let another account or service access a resource directly.
Choose a permissions boundary when developers may create roles but must not exceed a limit.
Choose an SCP to restrict what entire accounts or OUs can ever do, such as Regions or services.

values: Root, OU or account in Organizations
Every identity in member accounts, incl. root user
Stop privilege escalation by delegated admins
Does not affect the management account

iam-policy-types.diagram:
~~~groups
# Only two types grant access; the rest only set a maximum
[Effective permissions = Allow intersected with every limit]
Grant access: *Identity-based policy, *Resource-based policy
Limit only: Permissions boundary, SCP, Session policy
~~~

~~~decide
# What you need and which policy does it
Grant permissions to a Lambda role => Identity-based policy
Let another account read a bucket without assuming a role => Resource-based policy (bucket policy)
Developers create roles but cannot escalate privileges => Permissions boundary
Forbid a whole account from using unapproved Regions => SCP
~~~

keywords.trigger: Prevent all accounts from using a Region
Developers create IAM roles without privilege escalation
Allow another account to read a bucket
Explicit Deny vs Allow
Even the member account root user is restricted

cognito-pools.title: Cognito User Pool vs Identity Pool vs IAM Identity Center
cognito-pools.summary: All three deal with signing people in, but one authenticates app users, one hands out AWS credentials, and one is SSO for employees.
pick: Choose a User Pool to add sign-up and sign-in to an app and get JWTs.
Choose an Identity Pool when app users must call AWS services directly with temporary credentials.
Choose IAM Identity Center for employees to sign in once to many AWS accounts.

values: Exchange tokens for temporary AWS credentials
Workforce SSO to AWS accounts and apps
STS credentials mapped to IAM role
Session in accounts via permission sets
External IdP via SAML, SCIM provisioning

cognito-pools.diagram:
~~~flow
# Customers go through Cognito, employees through IAM Identity Center
Users -> Cognito User Pool -[JWT]-> Cognito Identity Pool -[STS credentials]-> S3
Employees -> IdP (Entra ID, Okta) -[SAML + SCIM]-> IAM Identity Center -[permission set]-> Many AWS accounts
~~~

~~~decide
# Exam keywords and the pick
App needs sign-up, sign-in and JWTs => Cognito User Pool
App users upload straight to S3 => Cognito Identity Pool
Unauthenticated guests call AWS with limited rights => Identity Pool (guest role)
Employees sign in once to many accounts => IAM Identity Center
~~~

keywords.trigger: Mobile app users upload directly to S3
Sign-up and sign-in for millions of app users
Employees use Microsoft Entra ID to access many accounts
Guest users with limited AWS access

kms-cloudhsm.title: KMS AWS managed key vs customer managed key vs CloudHSM
kms-cloudhsm.summary: All protect encryption keys; the difference is how much control you have over policy, rotation and the hardware itself.
pick: Choose an AWS managed key for default encryption with no management at all.
Choose a customer managed key when you need key policy control, cross-account sharing or disable/delete.
Choose CloudHSM when compliance requires a single-tenant HSM under your exclusive control.

values: You, in your own HSM cluster
You manage users and keys in the HSM
PKCS#11, JCE, CNG; KMS custom key store
High: you run HA across AZs

kms-cloudhsm.diagram:
~~~ladder
# More control means more operations
AWS managed key | AWS creates and rotates it, key policy not editable | No ops
Customer managed key | You own the key policy, grants, cross-account sharing | Low
CloudHSM | Single-tenant HSM, you hold the keys and run HA | High
~~~

~~~decide
# Exam requirements and the key to pick
Default encryption with nothing to manage => AWS managed key
Share an encrypted snapshot with another account => Customer managed key
Edit the key policy, disable or delete the key => Customer managed key
Single-tenant HSM under the company's exclusive control => CloudHSM
~~~

keywords.trigger: Dedicated, single-tenant hardware security module
Share encrypted snapshot with another account
Control key policy and audit key usage
Least operational overhead encryption
Same keys usable in multiple Regions

s3-encryption.title: S3 encryption options
s3-encryption.summary: Five ways to encrypt S3 objects that differ in who holds the key, who encrypts, and how much audit you get.
pick: Choose SSE-S3 for simple encryption at rest with no key management.
Choose SSE-KMS when you need key policy control and an audit trail of key usage.
Choose DSSE-KMS when a standard requires two independent layers of encryption.
Choose SSE-C when you must manage keys yourself but let S3 do the encryption.
Choose client-side encryption when AWS must never see plaintext data.

values: KMS request quotas; S3 Bucket Keys reduce calls
HTTPS required; AWS does not store key
Data is encrypted before leaving your app

s3-encryption.diagram:
~~~ladder
# The key moves from AWS into your hands
SSE-S3 | S3 manages the key, default for new objects | Default
SSE-KMS | Key in KMS, audited in CloudTrail | Audit
DSSE-KMS | Key in KMS, two layers of encryption | 2 layers
SSE-C | You send the key with each request, S3 encrypts | HTTPS
Client-side | The app encrypts before upload | DIY
~~~

~~~flow
# S3 Bucket Keys cut KMS calls for SSE-KMS
PutObject -[SSE-KMS]-> S3 -[calls KMS for every object]-> KMS (risk of throttling)
PutObject -[SSE-KMS + Bucket Key]-> S3 (temporary bucket-level key) -[far fewer calls]-> KMS
~~~

keywords.trigger: Audit who used the key
KMS throttling on high request rate
Dual-layer encryption requirement
Company provides its own key, not stored in AWS
Encrypt before uploading

secrets-vs-parameters.title: Secrets Manager vs SSM Parameter Store
secrets-vs-parameters.summary: Both store encrypted configuration values; the exam separates them by automatic rotation and cost.
pick: Choose Secrets Manager when credentials must rotate automatically or be replicated across Regions.
Choose Parameter Store for cheap configuration values and secrets without rotation needs.

values: Built-in (Lambda or managed rotation for RDS, Aurora...)
Paid per secret and API calls
Standard tier free; Advanced tier paid

secrets-vs-parameters.diagram:
~~~decide
# Choosing where to store a secret
DB password must rotate automatically => Secrets Manager
Secret must exist in the DR Region => Secrets Manager (replica secret)
Hierarchical config at the lowest cost => Parameter Store Standard
Simple secret with no rotation => Parameter Store SecureString
~~~

~~~flow
# How an app reads values at runtime
App -[GetParameter with WithDecryption]-> Parameter Store (SecureString) -[Decrypt]-> KMS
App -[GetSecretValue]-> Secrets Manager -[replicate]-> Replica secret in DR Region
~~~

keywords.trigger: Rotate RDS credentials automatically
Store configuration at lowest cost
Secret needed in a DR Region
Hierarchical config like /prod/app/db-url

security-detection.title: GuardDuty vs Inspector vs Macie vs Security Hub vs Detective
security-detection.summary: Five security services with similar names; each answers a different question: threats, vulnerabilities, sensitive data, posture, or root cause.
pick: Choose GuardDuty for continuous, managed threat detection with no agents.
Choose Inspector for automated vulnerability scanning of EC2, container images and Lambda.

# Detect, aggregate, then investigate
GuardDuty (threats) -> Security Hub (aggregated findings)
Inspector (vulnerabilities) -> Security Hub (aggregated findings)
Macie (PII in S3) -> Security Hub (aggregated findings)
GuardDuty (finding) -> Detective (root cause)
~~~

Logs and account activity: *GuardDuty, Detective
Software on workloads: *Inspector
Data in S3: *Macie
Findings from other services: *Security Hub
~~~

audit-tools.title: CloudTrail vs AWS Config vs CloudWatch Logs
audit-tools.summary: All three record "what happened"; the exam separates API calls, resource configuration, and application logs.
pick: Choose CloudTrail to audit who did what through the AWS API.
Choose AWS Config to track configuration history and enforce compliance rules.
Choose CloudWatch Logs to collect, search and alarm on application and system logs.

values: API calls: who, what, when, from where
Log lines from apps, OS, services
What did this SG look like last week? Is it compliant?
What errors did my app log?
Event history: 90 days of management events
Retention configurable, never expire by default
Metric filters to alarms, Logs Insights

~~~groups
# Each tool records something different
CloudTrail: Who called which API, When and from where
AWS Config: Resource configuration over time, *Config rules and remediation
CloudWatch Logs: App and OS logs, *Metric filter to alarm
~~~

~~~flow
# One event leaves a trace in each tool
Admin deletes an SG rule -[API call]-> CloudTrail (who, when, from where)
Admin deletes an SG rule -[configuration change]-> AWS Config (before and after, compliant?)
App hits an error -[writes log]-> CloudWatch Logs -[metric filter]-> CloudWatch alarm
~~~

keywords.trigger: Who made the API call
Detect and remediate non-compliant resources
Configuration at a point in time
Alarm on an error string in logs
Log files must not be tampered with

vpc-connectivity-options.title: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink vs Gateway endpoint
vpc-connectivity-options.summary: All keep traffic private, but they connect different things: whole networks, many networks, one service, or S3/DynamoDB.
pick: Choose VPC peering to link a few VPCs simply with no hub.
Choose Transit Gateway to connect many VPCs and on-premises networks transitively.
Choose PrivateLink to expose or consume one service privately, even with overlapping CIDRs.
Choose a gateway endpoint for free private access to S3 or DynamoDB from inside the VPC.

values: ENI with private IP; provider uses NLB
Prefix list entry in route table
Most AWS services, SaaS, your own

vpc-connectivity-options.diagram:
~~~groups
# Each option connects something different
VPC peering: Two VPCs 1:1, Not transitive
Transit Gateway: *Transitive hub, VPC + VPN + DX
PrivateLink: One service behind an NLB, Overlapping CIDRs are fine
Gateway endpoint: S3 and DynamoDB only, *Free
~~~

~~~decide
# Exam keywords and the pick
A few VPCs, simple and low cost => VPC peering
Hundreds of VPCs plus on-premises, transitive => Transit Gateway
Expose a service to customer VPCs with overlapping CIDRs => PrivateLink
Private subnet reaches S3 at no charge => Gateway endpoint
Private S3 access from on-premises => S3 interface endpoint
~~~

keywords.trigger: Hundreds of VPCs, simplify network
Expose a service to other VPCs with overlapping CIDRs
Private S3 access at no cost
Access S3 privately from on-premises

hybrid-connectivity.title: Site-to-Site VPN vs Direct Connect vs DX + VPN vs Client VPN
hybrid-connectivity.summary: All connect outside networks to AWS; the trade-off is speed of setup, consistent performance, encryption and who connects.
pick: Choose Site-to-Site VPN for fast, low-cost encrypted connectivity or as a backup for DX.
Choose Direct Connect for consistent latency and high, steady bandwidth.
Choose DX + VPN when you need DX performance and encryption in transit.
Choose Client VPN for remote employees connecting from laptops.

values: Variable, up to 1.25 Gbps per tunnel
Virtual interface to VGW, DX gateway or TGW

hybrid-connectivity.diagram:
~~~flow
# The paths from outside into AWS
Employee laptop -[TLS over the Internet]-> Client VPN endpoint -> VPC
Customer gateway -[IPsec over the Internet]-> VGW or Transit Gateway -> VPC
Data center -[dedicated line]-> DX location -[VIF]-> VPC
Data center -[IPsec over DX]-> Transit Gateway -> VPC
~~~

~~~ladder
# On-premises connection resiliency, lowest to highest
Single DX connection | One single point of failure | No redundancy
DX + Site-to-Site VPN | VPN over the Internet takes over when DX fails | Cost-effective
Two DX at two locations | Survives the loss of one location | High
Two DX at each of two locations | Survives device and location failures | Maximum
~~~

keywords.trigger: Connect quickly, encrypted, low cost

Remote workers access VPC resources
Maximum resilience for DX

multi-az-vs-replica.title: RDS Multi-AZ vs Read Replica vs Aurora Replica vs Aurora Global Database
multi-az-vs-replica.summary: All create database copies, but some are for availability, some for read scaling, and one for cross-Region DR.
pick: Choose RDS Multi-AZ to survive an AZ failure with automatic failover.
Choose RDS Read Replicas to offload read traffic or reports from the primary.
Choose Aurora Replicas for both read scaling and fast failover inside a Region.
Choose Aurora Global Database for cross-Region DR with very low RPO and RTO.

values: Multi-AZ DB cluster has readable standbys
RPO about 1 s, RTO under 1 minute

multi-az-vs-replica.diagram:
~~~flow
# Each kind of copy serves a different goal
RDS primary -[sync]-> Multi-AZ standby (other AZ, not readable)
RDS primary -[async]-> Read Replica (readable, manual promote)
Aurora writer -[shared cluster storage]-> Aurora Replica (readable, automatic failover)
Aurora primary Region -[replication under 1 second]-> Secondary Region (Global Database)
~~~

~~~ladder
# The scope of failure each option survives
Read Replica in the same Region | Offloads reads, manual promotion | No auto failover
RDS Multi-AZ | Instance or AZ failure, automatic failover | AZ
Aurora Replica | Automatic failover by priority tier, usually faster than RDS | AZ
Aurora Global Database | Whole-Region outage, RPO about 1 second | Region
~~~

keywords.trigger: Automatic failover if an AZ fails
Reporting queries slow down production
Region outage, RPO seconds, RTO under a minute
Low-latency reads for users in other Regions

keywords.trigger: Standby used for reads?
keywords.answer: No, Multi-AZ instance standby is not readable

messaging.title: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis Data Streams

pick: Choose SQS Standard to buffer and decouple work at any scale.

Producer -> SQS -[consumer polls]-> Consumer
Producer -> SNS -[push fan-out]-> Many SQS queues
AWS or SaaS event -> EventBridge -[content-based rule]-> Target
Producer -> Kinesis Data Streams -[read and replay]-> Many consumers
~~~

~~~decide
# Exam keywords and the pick
Buffer work and decouple tiers => SQS Standard
Strict order, no duplicates => SQS FIFO
One message to many subscribers => SNS
Route SaaS events by content => EventBridge
Many consumers replay real-time data => Kinesis Data Streams
~~~

dr-strategies.title: Disaster recovery strategies
dr-strategies.summary: Four strategies trade cost against RTO/RPO; questions give a target RTO/RPO and budget and expect the cheapest one that fits.
pick: Choose backup & restore when hours of downtime are acceptable and cost must be lowest.
Choose pilot light when data must be current but app servers can start after a disaster.
Choose warm standby when recovery must take minutes and a small copy can always run.
Choose multi-site active/active when downtime must be near zero regardless of cost.

values: Route 53, Aurora Global, DynamoDB global tables

dr-strategies.diagram:
~~~ladder
# Cheapest to most expensive, RTO shrinking
Backup & restore | Only backups in the DR Region | Hours
Pilot light | Data replicated, app turned off | Tens of minutes
Warm standby | A scaled-down stack is running | Minutes
Multi-site active/active | A full stack serving traffic | Near zero
~~~

~~~groups
# What is running in the DR Region
Backup & restore: Snapshots and backups, Nothing running
Pilot light: *Database replica, AMIs and IaC ready
Warm standby: *Database replica, *Scaled-down ASG, ALB
Multi-site active/active: *Full database, *Production stack, Route 53 splits traffic
~~~

keywords.trigger: Lowest cost, RTO of hours acceptable
Only the database runs in the DR Region
Scaled-down but functional copy
Zero downtime, both Regions serve traffic

route53-policies.summary: Seven policies that all return DNS answers; the trigger words are about location, latency, percentage or health.
pick: Choose Simple for one resource with no health checks.

Multiple values returned in random order

Set bias to grow or shrink area
Up to 8 healthy records; not a load balancer

Split traffic by percentage, canary => Weighted

load-balancers.title: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB

block-file-object.title: Block vs file vs object storage
block-file-object.summary: Every option "stores data for EC2", but they differ in access protocol, how many instances can share them, and whether data survives a stop.

EFS: a shared Linux file system across many instances and AZs that grows automatically.
FSx: Windows SMB file shares, HPC (Lustre), or lifting NetApp/ZFS file servers to AWS.
S3: objects, static files, backups, data lakes, unlimited storage accessed over the API.

Block (attached to an instance): *EBS (durable), Instance store (temporary)
File (many clients mount): *EFS (Linux NFS), FSx (SMB/Lustre/ONTAP/ZFS)
Object (over HTTPS API): *S3 (unlimited)
~~~

Temporary data, highest IOPS, loss acceptable => Instance store
Database on one EC2 instance, must be durable => EBS
Many Linux instances share files across AZs => EFS

~~~

databases.title: Choosing a database
databases.summary: All five store data, but they target different access patterns: relational OLTP, key-value at scale, analytics, or in-memory caching.

Aurora: MySQL/PostgreSQL apps needing more performance, fast failover or global replication.
DynamoDB: key-value access at any scale with consistent low latency and no servers.
Redshift: analytical SQL and BI dashboards over terabytes to petabytes.
ElastiCache: offload repeated reads or store sessions with sub-millisecond latency.

databases.diagram:
~~~decide

Standard relational, need Oracle or SQL Server => RDS
MySQL/PostgreSQL needing more speed, fast failover => Aurora

~~~

~~~

s3-classes.title: S3 storage classes
s3-classes.summary: Seven classes trade storage price against access speed, retrieval fees, minimum duration and resilience.
pick: Standard: frequently accessed data with no retrieval fees.

Standard-IA: rarely read data that must be available immediately and survive an AZ loss.
One Zone-IA: infrequent, easily re-created data where one-AZ resilience is acceptable.
Glacier Instant Retrieval: archive accessed about quarterly that still needs millisecond reads.
Glacier Flexible Retrieval: archives where minutes-to-hours restore is fine.
Glacier Deep Archive: lowest-cost long-term retention with restores within 12-48 hours.
